title: Paul O'Neill Starts With Safety
text:
In 1987 Paul O'Neill, a former government official, became chief executive of Alcoa, the American aluminum giant. Investors expected a new CEO to talk about profits, costs and markets.

At his first big meeting with investors and analysts in New York, O'Neill instead began by pointing out the emergency exits in the room. Then he said he wanted to talk about worker safety. Aluminum plants were dangerous places, and he announced that his goal was to make Alcoa the safest company in America, aiming for zero injuries. Charles Duhigg, who told the story in The Power of Habit, reports that some investors left convinced the company was in trouble.

O'Neill required that any injury be reported to him within twenty-four hours, together with a plan to prevent it from happening again. To meet that demand, information had to flow quickly from the shop floor to the top, and managers and workers had to examine every process closely. The changes spread from safety into quality and efficiency.

Alcoa's injury rate fell sharply. By the time O'Neill left in 2000 to become Treasury Secretary, the company's profits and market value had grown many times over.
lesson: Pick one goal everyone can agree on and pursue it relentlessly. The habits it demands can change the whole organization.
location: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and New York, USA
source: Charles Duhigg, The Power of Habit (2012), chapter 4; O'Neill's speeches and interviews
caveat: How much of Alcoa's financial success came from the safety focus rather than market conditions is debated.
